rewrites.summary:
Same-sex conduct is legal and no law targets trans presence, so Chiapas itself has no statute criminalising or restricting trans visitors. Chiapas is one of ten of Mexico's 32 states that had still created no legal gender recognition procedure as of March 2025, despite supreme-court doctrine establishing the right; the practical consequence is permanently mismatched identity documents for trans people - the legal fact most relevant to a visitor, since document mismatch triggers questioning at checkpoints, banks and clinics - with no local administrative cure, only the courts able to order recognition case by case.

No Chiapas-specific violence series, incidents or enforcement pattern is documented in the surviving sources, so practical safety here rests on the national baseline rather than any verified local threat or protection.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Rights reporting on a neighbouring non-reforming state - an unsolved killing of a trans activist, health staff outting patients, no hate-motivation provisions - illustrates the institutional climate such refusal sustains. The capital's 2024 transfemicide law marks the national reform benchmark this state has not followed.
rewrites.localsOnly: The absence of a legal gender recognition procedure bites hardest on residents' documents and registry dealings; visitors use home documents and never apply locally.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: General cartel violence, kidnapping and theft drive foreign travel advisories for parts of Mexico and affect all travellers equally; they do not move trans-specific risk here. The visitor picture rests on the national framework and a neighbouring state's reporting; no state-specific enforcement, incident or screening data is documented in the surviving sources.

Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and no hostile state ordinance is documented in the surviving sources.

The surviving audited sources for this record document no state-specific incident series; practical safety rests on the national backdrop, which remains violent and impunity-prone for trans people.

rewrites.summary:
Same-sex conduct is not criminalised in Colima, and no law targets trans presence. Legal gender recognition across the country remains an unresolved state-by-state mosaic that courts have pressed state legislatures to complete, and the country overall is one of Latin America's deadliest settings for trans people, with high impunity - the operative backdrop a visitor stands under here.

No Colima-specific law, procedure, ordinance or incident series is documented in the audited record, so neither verified local protection nor verified local hostility can be claimed for visitors.
